title: Joint Formal Opinion 2024-200 — Ethical Issues Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence
pub: Pennsylvania Bar Association / Philadelphia Bar Association
author: Pennsylvania Bar Association Committee on Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility · Philadelphia Bar Association Professional Guidance Committee

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
st.an: The opinion accepts that AI use leaves existing competence and supervisory duties intact and that responsibility for misconduct is conditional rather than automatic. It materially develops the cluster by proposing a task-specific test: assess whether an AI tool can satisfy the professional rules to the same extent as a human performing the same work.
qs: Thus, when contemplating the appropriate use of generative AI, lawyers should consider whether an AI tool can satisfy the Rules of Professional Conduct to the same extent as a human hired to complete the same tasks.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The opinion materially develops the cluster’s protection-and-accountability analysis by providing concrete disciplinary examples showing that lawyers remain responsible for verifying AI-generated authorities and may face sanctions or suspension for unchecked reliance. It does not address whether cheaper AI assistance improves access to justice overall.
qs: The Court determined that the lawyers “abandoned their responsibilities” when they submitted the AI-written brief and “then continued to stand by the fake opinions after the judicial orders called their existence into question.” Both the individual attorneys and their law firm were fined $5,000 each.
The attorney did not cite or check any of the case references generated by ChatGPT, and he solely relied on the technology to create his brief without any review.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The opinion directly supports conditional AI assistance under existing professional duties while preserving lawyers’ responsibility for competence, substantive verification and confidentiality. Its discussion of differing court-specific disclosure and certification orders also aligns with the cluster’s central contrast among regulatory approaches.
qs: The Committees believe that, with appropriate safeguards, lawyers can utilize artificial intelligence in accordance with the Pennsylvania Rules of Professional Conduct.
These tools do not replace personal reviews of cases, statutes, and other legislative materials.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The opinion supports the cluster’s core distinction between permissible AI assistance and lawyers’ continuing responsibility for accurate filings. Its reported incidents show lawyers signing AI-assisted briefs containing fabricated authorities and facing consequences, while serving as illustrations rather than empirical measures of overall model reliability. Its separate discussion of bias is complementary but outside the cluster’s principal citation-error proposition.
qs: Lawyers have fallen victim to hallucinations and biases, signing their names to briefs authored entirely by or with the assistance of AI, which included some nonexistent cases.

The lawyer ultimately admitted that the source of the legal opinions had         “revealed itself to be unreliable.” 5     •   A New York lawyer filed an appellate reply brief citing a nonexistent case, and was referred         to the court’s Grievance Panel.

st.t: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
st.an: The opinion supports the cluster’s human-accountable, assistive model by treating existing professional duties as unchanged by AI and highlighting verification, competence, bias and misplaced reliance. It also confirms that some courts impose disclosure and citation-verification requirements, while correctly presenting these as jurisdiction-specific rather than universal.
qs: The Guidelines explain that AI does not change the fundamental duties of legal professionals to be aware of new applications and potential challenges in the discharge of such responsibilities.

He or she must, in a clear and plain factual         statement, disclose that generative AI has been used in any way in the preparation         of the filing or correspondence and certify that each and every citation to the law         or the record in the filing has been verified as authentic and accurate.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s core view that AI remains supervised assistance: lawyers retain responsibility for accuracy, legal reasoning, citation verification and confidentiality, while judicial guidance emphasizes technological competence and awareness of bias and accuracy risks. Its discussion of disclosure reflects particular court orders rather than claiming a universal rule, consistent with the cluster’s jurisdiction-specific treatment.
qs: When citing legal authorities such as case law, statutes,        regulations, or scholarly articles, lawyers should verify that the citations accurately reflect        the content they are referencing.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s core proposition: generative AI can create substantive legal work product and improve efficiency, but its outputs may be unreliable and remain subject to lawyers’ verification, technological competence and existing professional duties. It supplies ethical guidance rather than comparative performance evidence or a materially different framework.
qs: Generative AI differs from non-generative AI because it creates content, and it is the creation of content that necessitates heightened awareness by lawyers.
Because generative AI creates content, however, lawyers have an obligation to verify that the citations are correct and that they accurately summarize the cases or other information cited.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: existing professional duties continue to govern AI-assisted legal work, lawyers remain personally accountable, and verification must cover both citation authenticity and substantive support. It permits bounded AI use with safeguards and reports AI-specific court orders without treating disclosure or prohibition as a universal requirement.
qs: Regardless, whether a baseless argument is made with the assistance of AI or not is irrelevant; the lawyer is responsible.
Because generative AI creates content, however, lawyers have an obligation to verify that the citations are correct and that they accurately summarize the cases or other information cited.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The opinion supports the cluster’s emphasis on human verification, professional judgment and accountability by requiring lawyers to check AI-generated legal work and safeguard clients. Its scope is lawyer use rather than direct-to-consumer access, so it does not resolve the cluster’s broader comparison between imperfect AI assistance and no assistance.
qs: When citing legal authorities such as case law, statutes,        regulations, or scholarly articles, lawyers should verify that the citations accurately reflect        the content they are referencing.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s copilot framing: generative AI may improve productivity, but its generated content requires heightened scrutiny, independent verification and continued lawyer accountability. It also reinforces that safeguards must address confidentiality and bias, while offering no evidence that grounding eliminates probabilistic error or that quality gains are consistent.
qs: Because generative AI creates content, however, lawyers have an obligation to verify that the citations are correct and that they accurately summarize the cases or other information cited.
The Committees believe that, with appropriate safeguards, lawyers can utilize artificial intelligence in accordance with the Pennsylvania Rules of Professional Conduct.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: generative AI can assist legal work, but hallucinations and inaccurate summaries make lawyer verification necessary before reliance. Its bias discussion also aligns with the cluster’s broader warning that reliability extends beyond fabricated citations, though it provides no empirical error-rate or net-productivity evidence.
qs: Because generative AI creates content, however, lawyers have an obligation to verify that the citations are correct and that they accurately summarize the cases or other information cited.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s core proposition: AI can automate routine legal tasks and improve efficiency while lawyers retain higher-value judgment and professional responsibility. It also reinforces verification, technological competence, continuing training and confidentiality safeguards as necessary boundaries against hallucination and overreliance. It does not materially address the cluster’s apprenticeship or labour-market claims.
qs: AI technology has facilitated the automation of routine legal tasks, allowing legal professionals to focus on higher-value work requiring human expertise and judgment.
Because generative AI creates content, however, lawyers have an obligation to verify that the citations are correct and that they accurately summarize the cases or other information cited.

st.t: Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that lawyers remain accountable for AI-assisted filings and must verify accuracy. Its sanctions examples also reinforce that consequences turn on unchecked fabricated authority and post-filing conduct, while its discussion of Judge Starr is correctly framed as a judge-specific certification regime rather than a universal rule.
qs: 6 ^LLawyers are, therefore, facing disciplinary actions, both before judges and disciplinary authorities, for using AI technology without taking appropriate steps to ensure its accuracy and that their clients are receiving effective representation with its use.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that existing professional duties remain the ethical foundation for legal AI use and require active human scrutiny. It applies competence, confidentiality, communication, accuracy, verification and fee obligations to AI-assisted work without treating AI as either inherently reliable or categorically impermissible.
qs: This opinion will clarify how our existing ethical rules impact the proper use of this technology.
They also remain responsible for their work product and must verify the accuracy and sufficiency of research performed by generative AI.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The opinion strongly supports the cluster’s core copilot framing: AI may improve efficiency, but lawyers must understand its risks, substantively verify outputs, protect confidentiality and retain professional judgment and responsibility. It does not empirically determine whether verification consumes the resulting efficiency gains.
qs: (1) understand the technology and how it works, (2) understand the benefits of the technology, (3) understand the risks of the technology, (4) check and verify all citations and the material cited, and (5) especially in cases where the benefits outweigh the risks, have an obligation to educate the client and seek their informed consent to use the technology.

•   Exercising Professional Judgment: Lawyers must exercise their professional judgment        in conjunction with AI-generated content, and recognize that AI is a tool that assists but        does not replace legal expertise and analysis.

st.an: The opinion directly accepts the cluster’s core proposition: AI remains an assistive tool, lawyers retain professional judgment and accountability, and verification must confirm not only citation accuracy but also sound legal reasoning and substantive support. Its advisory, Pennsylvania-specific status is consistent with the cluster’s jurisdictional caveat.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion supports selective, human-led deployment: it recognises efficiency gains while rejecting autonomous substitution, requiring lawyers to retain professional judgment, verify outputs and comply with existing duties such as competence, confidentiality and supervision. Its emphasis is ethical governance rather than empirical measurement of jagged capability or organisational redesign.

kp.k: AI shifts routine work toward higher-value human tasks
kp.d: The Committees assert that AI supports research, contract analysis, document review, case management and routine automation, while generative AI adds drafting, summarization and synthesis. They describe efficiency gains and greater attention to strategy and client needs, but provide no quantified productivity or employment evidence.
qs: AI technology has facilitated the automation of routine legal tasks, allowing legal professionals to focus on higher-value work requiring human expertise and judgment.

It can assist lawyers by automating document drafting, preparing summaries, analyzing and synthesizing large volumes of documents and other information, optimizing efficiency, and allowing for more focused attention on legal strategy and client needs.

kp.k: Content generation creates heightened verification obligations
kp.d: The opinion distinguishes generative AI from established uses such as technology-assisted review and research indexing. Lawyers must personally check citations, their relevance and the accuracy of the underlying propositions rather than rely on plausible generated text.
qs: Generative AI differs from non-generative AI because it creates content, and it is the creation of content that necessitates heightened awareness by lawyers.
Because generative AI creates content, however, lawyers have an obligation to verify that the citations are correct and that they accurately summarize the cases or other information cited.
These tools do not replace personal reviews of cases, statutes, and other legislative materials.

kp.k: Existing Pennsylvania duties govern AI use
kp.d: The Committees frame AI as raising familiar ethical issues under existing Pennsylvania Rules of Professional Conduct, including competence, confidentiality, candor, supervision, communication, conflicts and unauthorized practice. They conclude that safeguarded AI use is permissible; this is advisory interpretation, not a binding court or disciplinary ruling.
qs: This opinion will clarify how our existing ethical rules impact the proper use of this technology.
The Committees believe that, with appropriate safeguards, lawyers can utilize artificial intelligence in accordance with the Pennsylvania Rules of Professional Conduct.
CAVEAT: The foregoing opinion is advisory only and is not binding on the Disciplinary Board of the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania or any other Court.

kp.k: Technological competence requires understanding and continuing education
kp.d: Under Pennsylvania Rule 1.1, the opinion says lawyers choosing AI must understand its operation, benefits and risks, verify materials and educate clients. It also recommends continuing education and training, extending the competence expected of traditional legal methods to relevant technological tools.
qs: Lawyers must be proficient in using technological tools to the same extent they are in employing traditional methods.
Lawyers must engage in continuing legal education and other training to stay informed about ethical issues and best practices for using AI in legal practice.

kp.k: Clients need explanations and potentially informed consent
kp.d: The opinion interprets Rule 1.4 as requiring discussion of generative AI's benefits, risks and limits and a joint determination of whether its use serves client objectives. Its competence discussion calls for education and informed consent, especially where benefits outweigh risks, while its concluding guidance describes consent as necessary for certain tools when warranted.
qs: Rule 1.4 requires the lawyer to inform the client of the benefits, risks, and limits of the use of generative AI.
In conjunction with the client, the lawyer must also determine whether the permissible use of generative AI would serve the client’s objectives in the representation.
If necessary, they should obtain client consent before using certain AI tools.

kp.k: Confidentiality safeguards must prevent cross-client information leakage
kp.d: The Committees warn that developing language models without safeguards such as ethical walls may use information from one representation to inform another, implicating duties to current and former clients. Lawyers must investigate access and security and avoid entering confidential information into inadequately protected systems; the opinion applies reasoning from earlier cloud, email and smartphone guidance.
qs: Therefore, a lawyer must not input any confidential information of a client into AI that lacks adequate confidentiality and security protections.

When using AI, a lawyer must ensure that any client information and materials remain confidential and safeguard that information to ensure that it is protected from breaches, data loss, and other risks.

kp.d: The opinion reports fabricated-authority incidents in Mata v. Avianca, Park v. Kim and Colorado disciplinary proceedings as illustrations of failures to verify, not measured model error rates. It describes a Grievance Panel referral in Park, sanctions in Mata and a one-year-and-one-day suspension in People v. Crabill, where it says the lawyer relied on generated cases without review.
qs: A New York lawyer filed an appellate reply brief citing a nonexistent case, and was referred to the court’s Grievance Panel.
In People v. Crabill 11, an attorney was suspended for one year and one day for using cases created by ChatGPT that were not actual cases.

Lawyers are, therefore, facing disciplinary actions, both before judges and disciplinary authorities, for using AI technology without taking appropriate steps to ensure its accuracy and that their clients are receiving effective representation with its use.

kp.k: Court-specific disclosure and verification requirements are emerging
kp.d: The opinion reports that some courts require disclosure or certification concerning AI-assisted filings. Its Eastern District of Pennsylvania example requires disclosure of any generative AI use and certification that every citation is authentic and accurate. The quoted Texas standing order requires certification of either no generative drafting or human accuracy checks using print reporters or traditional databases; these are judge-specific requirements, not a universal prohibition.
qs: Some Courts are mandating certain attorney disclosures and verifications when submitting any document to the Court that may be generated in whole or in part by some form of AI program or application.

He or she must, in a clear and plain factual statement, disclose that generative AI has been used in any way in the preparation of the filing or correspondence and certify that each and every citation to the law or the record in the filing has been verified as authentic and accurate.

kp.k: Lawyers retain responsibility and must remedy false evidence
kp.d: The opinion applies meritorious-claims and candor duties regardless of whether AI produced the argument. Lawyers must proactively avoid false statements and evidence, and react with reasonable remedial measures when AI-altered or invented evidence is discovered.
qs: Regardless, whether a baseless argument is made with the assistance of AI or not is irrelevant; the lawyer is responsible.

The full version of this Comment is focused on a false statement by a client; however, a lawyer has an obligation to ensure that evidence has not been altered or invented from whole cloth by an AI tool.
A lawyer must be both proactive and reactive in not presenting false statements or false evidence to a tribunal.

kp.k: AI requires supervision analogous to human assistance
kp.d: The Committees connect firm-level controls under Rule 5.1 to supervision of AI use by lawyers. They argue by analogy that Rule 5.3 should apply with equal force where AI functions like a human, asking whether the tool can meet the professional standards expected of a person performing the same task.
qs: The same ethical rules that apply to lawyers who employ or retain paralegals, junior associates, or outside consultants applies to lawyers who utilize AI.
While Rule 5.3 applies to “non-lawyers” and “persons,” where AI is able to function like a human, the Rule should apply with the same force.

kp.d: The opinion treats AI as assistance rather than substitution for legal expertise. In its unauthorized-practice discussion, it suggests that a nonlawyer programmer may implicate Rule 5.5 and directs lawyers to ensure licensed-attorney involvement in legal advice and tasks requiring legal judgment. That programmer proposition is the Committees' stated possibility, not a reported adjudication.
qs: To the extent that the AI programmer is not a lawyer, the programmer may violate Rule 5.5 regarding the unauthorized practice of law.
To avoid the UPL, lawyers must ensure that AI does not give legal advice or engage in tasks that require legal judgment or expertise, without the involvement of a licensed attorney.
There must always be a human element in the legal work product to ensure that lawyers are upholding their ethical obligations.

kp.k: Bias prevention extends to training data
kp.d: The opinion attributes AI bias to input data and gives a conditional criminal-risk-assessment example in which disproportionate high-risk flags could produce harsher sentences for marginalized communities. Its recommendation requires accurate, unbiased and ethically sourced training data, but it supplies neither measured bias findings nor an implementation method for lawyers to establish these properties.
qs: To the contrary, AI has biases that are the result of the data input into them.

If the algorithm disproportionately flags individuals from marginalized communities as high-risk, it could lead to unjust outcomes such as harsher sentences, perpetuating systemic biases within the legal system.
Lawyers must ensure that the data used to train AI models is accurate, unbiased, and ethically sourced to prevent perpetuating biases or inaccuracies in AI-generated content.

kp.k: Efficiency gains require reasonable, disclosed AI expenses
kp.d: The Committees connect AI's time-saving potential to billing duties, requiring reasonable AI-related expenses and appropriate client disclosure. They do not prescribe a pricing model, quantify savings or analyze changes to associate leverage.
qs: AI has tremendous time-saving capabilities.
Lawyers must, therefore, ensure that AI-related expenses are reasonable and appropriately disclosed to clients.

kp.k: Firm policies and insurance may constrain adoption
kp.d: The opinion reports internal firm policies governing AI use for documents containing sensitive information and asserts that some malpractice carriers exclude AI use while many policies restrict document preparation. It provides no carrier names, policy examples or prevalence data.
qs: To address these concerns, for example, some firms are implementing internal policies on whether a lawyer can use AI (and programs such as ChatGPT) when creating pleadings or other documents that may contain sensitive client information.

Additionally, some legal malpractice insurance carriers will not insure for AI’s use, and many policies now limit firms that are covered by them from using AI to prepare any documents, especially those that are being filed with a Court.

kp.k: Other jurisdictions emphasize continuing professional accountability
kp.d: The opinion identifies risk awareness and compliance with existing professional duties as common themes across other jurisdictions. It reports Florida's 2024 conditions on confidentiality, competence, billing and advertising; California's 2023 warning about persuasive outputs encouraging overreliance; New Jersey's 2024 reaffirmation of core duties; and Michigan's 2023 guidance on judicial technological competence. These are attributed external positions rather than new Pennsylvania rules.
qs: In every jurisdiction that has issued guidance or made recommendations concerning the use of AI, there is one common theme: Lawyers must recognize the risks and benefits of AI technology.

If they choose to use AI, particularly generative AI, they must understand its strengths and weaknesses and employ it consistent with their ethical obligations under the Rules of Professional Conduct.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The joint Committees describe AI as already transforming legal workflows through automation and greater efficiency, while insisting that it augments rather than replaces lawyers’ judgment.
pts.d: The Pennsylvania and Philadelphia Bar Association Committees claim that AI supports legal research, contract analysis, document review, case management and outcome prediction. Generative AI extends these capabilities to drafting, summarization and synthesis of large volumes of information. They claim these tools save time, support better-informed decisions and allow lawyers to concentrate on strategy, complex tasks and client needs. They also identify concrete constraints on these gains: generated authorities and evidence can be fabricated; biased systems can produce discriminatory outcomes; inadequately protected systems can expose confidential information or use one representation’s information in another. Lawyers remain responsible for output and must undertake human verification, supervision, professional judgment and client communication. The Committees describe court disclosure requirements, disciplinary consequences, firm policies and insurance restrictions as current responses to AI use. They link time savings to reasonable, disclosed expenses, but do not predict a shift away from hourly billing, lawyer displacement or changes in staffing structures.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The opinion relies on professional-rule interpretation, documented court incidents and examples of established technology, rather than quantitative evidence of productivity or market effects.
pts.d: For existing AI applications, the Committees describe technology-assisted review, predictive coding, document indexing and natural-language legal research, citing the Sedona Conference’s definition of TAR. Their broader claims about time savings, better service and improved decisions are not supported by measured productivity data or comparative benchmarks. For risks and consequences, they cite Mata v. Avianca, Park v. Kim, People v. Crabill and a Ninth Circuit brief-striking incident, as well as standing orders requiring disclosure or human verification. These are examples of failures and institutional responses, not measured hallucination rates. The bias discussion offers a conditional criminal-risk-assessment example rather than a specific empirical study. The confidentiality and supervision conclusions rest principally on the Committees’ interpretation of Pennsylvania’s Rules of Professional Conduct, prior Pennsylvania opinions and guidance from other jurisdictions. The statements about firm policies and insurance restrictions have no named policy examples or quantified supporting evidence in the supplied text. This is an advisory ethics opinion, not a binding judicial determination; quoted outside authorities supply context and support rather than independent claims by the joint Committees.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern capabilities and consequences already present as of May 2024; permissible benefits are conditional on safeguards and continuing human oversight.
pts.d: The opinion, dated 22 May 2024, presents conventional AI as long established and generative AI as a recent extension, identifying ChatGPT’s November 2022 release as a turning point. Court incidents and other jurisdictions’ guidance largely date from 2023–2024. It supplies no forecast horizon, adoption rate or quantified future productivity projection. Its central qualification is that lawyers choosing AI must understand its benefits and risks, check citations and cited materials, protect confidential information, supervise its use and retain legal judgment. The Committees require communication about benefits, risks and limitations; their competence discussion calls for informed consent, while the final best-practices list says consent should be obtained if necessary for certain tools. Their UPL discussion insists on licensed-attorney involvement in advice and tasks requiring legal judgment. Productivity gains are therefore framed as conditional rather than as authorization for autonomous legal service delivery.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are practicing lawyers, law-firm supervisors, clients and courts; the opinion also identifies potential consequences for marginalized communities and nonlawyer AI programmers.
pts.d: Lawyers may complete routine work faster and devote more attention to complex work, but remain accountable for checking output, technological competence, confidentiality and truthful submissions. Partners, managers and supervisory lawyers must provide measures and oversight analogous to those governing junior associates, paralegals and consultants; this is an accountability analogy, not a staffing-replacement prediction. Firms face sanctions exposure, internal-policy decisions and asserted insurance limitations. Clients may receive more focused service but face confidentiality, conflicts, inaccurate-representation and expense risks, making communication and reasonable billing important. Courts face false authorities and potentially invented evidence and are responding through filing requirements and sanctions. Marginalized communities are identified as potentially harmed by biased criminal-risk assessments. The Committees also suggest that nonlawyer programmers may encounter unauthorized-practice concerns, and require licensed-lawyer involvement in legal advice. The opinion does not differentiate effects by firm size, enterprise versus individual clients, or legal market segment.
